title: Pulmonary acinus: alveoli and gas-exchange barrier
description: From terminal bronchiole to alveolar sac, type I/II pneumocytes, macrophages and the air–blood barrier.

questions.question: What is a pulmonary acinus?
questions.answer: An acinus is the lung region distal to a terminal bronchiole where respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli participate in gas exchange. It is a microanatomical unit, not a whole lung lobe.

questions.question: How do Type I and Type II alveolar cells differ?
questions.answer: Type I pneumocytes are thin squamous lining cells specialized for gas exchange. Type II pneumocytes are plumper cells that make surfactant and help replenish the alveolar lining.

questions.question: What is the alveolar–capillary barrier?
questions.answer: It is the thin interface separating air in an alveolus from blood in a nearby capillary, involving alveolar epithelium, shared basement membranes and capillary endothelium. Its short diffusion distance supports gas exchange.

questions.question: Are alveolar macrophages attached to the wall?
questions.answer: Alveolar macrophages can move on the air-facing surface of alveoli and engulf inhaled particles and debris. They are not the same as Type I or Type II epithelial cells.

questions.question: Is the Type I cell image a histology photograph?
questions.answer: No. The separate alveolar cell view is a digital teaching illustration. The thin lining and plumper Type II cell are depicted for learning, not presented as a clinical slide or a literal lung-image zoom.
